01-reality-of-ownership.question: How much does it cost to run a superyacht per year?
01-reality-of-ownership.answer: Annual running cost on a 40 to 50 metre yacht operated privately at moderate use is typically 12 to 15 percent of purchase price, not the folkloric 10 percent. On a 50 metre new-build motor yacht that runs to roughly EUR 4 to 6 million per year. Crew is the dominant line at 30 to 40 percent of total operating cost. Maintenance, insurance, berths, fuel, management, and compliance fill the rest. Charter operation, larger size, and older age all push the figure higher. The running cost calculator on this site tests a buyer’s own figures against MYBA, Pantaenius, and Quay Crew published data.

01-reality-of-ownership.question: Is the 10 percent rule for yacht ownership accurate?
01-reality-of-ownership.answer: The 10 percent rule, that annual operating cost equals roughly 10 percent of purchase price, is a folkloric figure with no traceable origin. It is roughly correct for new, mid-sized, lightly used yachts, but wrong for most readers of The First Owner’s Reference. As the yacht loses value the percentage rises as a matter of arithmetic, since running cost depends on size and complexity, not on what the yacht is worth. YachtBuyer in published analysis calls the rule at best obsolete or even misleading for older or larger crewed vessels. A sound budget figure is 12 to 15 percent for a typical 40 to 50 metre new build privately operated at moderate use.

01-reality-of-ownership.question: How much does a superyacht depreciate?
01-reality-of-ownership.answer: Broker-published figures put the first-year loss at 10 to 15 percent (Yatco) or 10 to 20 percent (IYC), followed by about 5 percent a year on Yatco’s figures. Together they put the typical loss by year five at about 30 to 50 percent of the purchase price. The curve flattens after year five. Quality builders such as Feadship, Lürssen, Royal Huisman, Vitters, and Baltic Yachts hold value materially better, with single-digit percentage losses possible after year five. There is no peer-reviewed academic study of yacht depreciation; all published curves are broker-aggregated and self-reported, so the figures are indicative.

01-reality-of-ownership.question: Can charter income offset yacht ownership cost?
01-reality-of-ownership.answer: For the median yacht in the median programme, the published arithmetic does not bear out the claim that charter pays for ownership. BOAT International published case studies show a 48 metre motor yacht at 7 charter weeks per year breaking roughly even on running cost; a 47 metre sailing yacht at 9 weeks losing EUR 444,000; an 85 metre motor yacht at 8 weeks losing EUR 430,000. The one clearly profitable case is a 60 metre concept modelled by Hill Robinson for charter, not a trading yacht, and it assumes premium rates and prime-season weeks given to charter. In most charter programmes, income offsets part of the cost of ownership but does not cover it.

01-reality-of-ownership.question: How many weeks per year does a yacht owner typically use the boat?
01-reality-of-ownership.answer: Practitioner estimates place typical use at 4 to 8 weeks per year, with committed users reaching 12 to 16 weeks. The Superyacht Report’s OpEx Survey (Q2 2026), answered by captains of 28 to 83 metre yachts, records owners aboard an average of 17 weeks a year on private programmes; the difference reflects the samples. This publication treats 12 weeks of intended use as the point at which ownership starts to make sense. The first task before any acquisition is an honest estimate of intended use, tested against the buyer’s actual calendar for the next five years. Below 12 weeks of intended use, charter and fractional access cover the same calendar at lower fixed cost.

02-reading-the-market.question: How big is the superyacht market in 2026?
02-reading-the-market.answer: Knight Frank’s Wealth Report 2026, using BOAT International data, estimates 2025 sales of yachts over 24 metres at USD 8.5 billion on asking prices, a 70 percent rise on the prior year. Edmiston’s 2025 review, which counts brokerage sales of yachts over 30 metres only, records more than EUR 7.1 billion. The two figures measure different things. The 2026 BOAT International Global Order Book lists 1,093 yachts of 24 metres and above on order or in build, down from 1,138 in 2025, the second consecutive annual decline by unit count. Average length on the order book has risen to 40.8 metres and average tonnage to 551 GT, up from 40.0 metres and 507 GT a year earlier. Italy now builds more yachts than any other country: 568 units, 52 percent of the global order book by units.

02-reading-the-market.question: Which yards are sold out for new build superyachts?
02-reading-the-market.answer: Top-tier yards are at capacity. Lürssen’s large-yacht capacity is committed several years ahead and was enlarged by the Nobiskrug yard in 2025. Feadship slot availability was reported in 2026 as extending to 2028 to 2029. Oceanco delivered the 111 metre DreAMBoat in November 2025, about 18 months faster than a conventional custom build of that size. Heesen runs a speculative-build model with hulls in build for delivery between 2026 and 2028. Mid-tier yards have varying capacity. The major decision for a first-time buyer is whether to take a brokerage hull now, take a slot at a mid-tier yard with capacity, or wait three to four years for a top-tier delivery.

02-reading-the-market.question: Why is the United States driving the 2026 yacht market?
02-reading-the-market.answer: Knight Frank’s Wealth Report 2026 names US demand as the biggest catalyst of the 2025 rise, with US buyers rushing to close before the year end once the One Big Beautiful Bill Act reintroduced a 100 percent depreciation bonus. The Knight Frank Wealth Report 2026 records that 41 percent of new UHNWIs were created in the United States and forecasts the US share rising to 41 percent of the world’s UHNW population by 2031. Knight Frank also cites BOAT International data: US buyers account for 45 to 50 percent of yacht transactions, and sales of yachts over 70 metres rose 60 percent year on year.

02-reading-the-market.question: How is wealth being created and transferred for yacht buyers?
02-reading-the-market.answer: The Knight Frank Wealth Sizing Model places the global UHNWI population (above USD 30 million) at 713,626 in 2026, up 162,191 over five years. Capgemini’s World Wealth Report 2025 records USD 83.5 trillion of wealth being inherited by Gen X, millennials, and Gen Z by 2048, with 81 percent of next-generation HNWIs intending to switch from their parents’ wealth management firm within one to two years of inheritance. Many readers of The First Owner’s Reference will be a principal who has recently sold a business, or an heir reviewing the advisers their parents used.

03-how-the-industry-works.question: Who pays the yacht broker commission?
03-how-the-industry-works.answer: On a brokerage transaction, the seller pays the commission from the sale proceeds, regardless of which broker introduces the buyer. The buyer is not invoiced. The IYBA standard is a flat 10 percent of the sale price; MYBA uses a sliding scale. The consequence is that the broker guiding the buyer is paid only if the sale closes, and paid by the other side. The buyer can ask for that payment, and any referral fees from suppliers the broker introduces, to be disclosed in writing, and can engage an independent adviser whose income does not depend on the sale closing.

03-how-the-industry-works.question: What is dual agency in a yacht transaction?
03-how-the-industry-works.answer: Dual agency is when a single brokerage represents both the buyer and the seller. California requires explicit dual-agency disclosure, and Florida’s transactional-brokerage rules dilute full agency duties by default. The IYBA Purchase and Sale Agreement contains a dual-agency clause that amounts to pre-emptive consent. Disclosure beyond that clause, including any retrocession arrangements with introducing parties, is not always volunteered. The book’s standard is written disclosure of the role and the payment; a buyer who wants an adviser acting only for them engages an independent adviser (owner’s representative).

03-how-the-industry-works.question: What is a retrocession in yacht industry?
03-how-the-industry-works.answer: A retrocession is a commission rebate paid privately between counterparties, typically from a yard, supplier, or management company back to a referring broker, captain, or adviser. OnboardOnline’s legal column states that referral fees are legal only if disclosed, must be reflected in the closing statement to seller and buyer, and that undisclosed payments to a captain are potentially criminal. No equivalent rule compels a brokerage to disclose retrocessions on ongoing services. Asking each introduced party for written disclosure of every referral relationship and retrocession arrangement is the buyer’s protection.

03-how-the-industry-works.question: Should I trust the captain’s recommendation on broker, surveyor, or yard?
03-how-the-industry-works.answer: A captain’s recommendation merits the same disclosure question as any other. The captain may have prior commercial relationships with brokers, yards, suppliers, and management companies that continue into employment. The candidate’s introduction route, prior commercial relationships, and pay structure (straight salary versus bonus, charter share, or referral-related elements) are all worth establishing in writing before the captain is hired. A candidate who agrees with everything is easy to interview; one who asks difficult questions about the owner’s plans is often the better hire.

04-acquisition-process.question: How long does it take to buy a superyacht?
04-acquisition-process.answer: The acquisition window for a brokerage hull is typically 12 to 24 weeks from shortlist to closing. Most of the work is done in the first ten weeks: shortlisting from at least two brokerages plus an independent off-market scan, pre-purchase survey by an independently engaged surveyor, sea trial with the buyer’s own captain candidate present, and contract drafting under independent counsel. An early close suits the seller and the parties paid on completion, while the buyer carries whatever was not checked; three further weeks of due diligence cost little and often surface issues worth more than the delay.

04-acquisition-process.question: Do I need a pre-purchase survey before buying a yacht?
04-acquisition-process.answer: Yes. A pre-purchase survey by an independently engaged surveyor is essential to any acquisition. Cost on a 40 to 50 metre yacht runs USD 25,000 to 60,000 inclusive of paint specialist and class-society inspector, over four to seven days afloat plus haul-out. Recognised firms include Ward & McKenzie and Patton Marine. Renegotiation on every material deficiency the survey finds is standard practice. The seller’s most recent survey is not a substitute.

04-acquisition-process.question: What is a Memorandum of Agreement on a yacht sale?
04-acquisition-process.answer: The MOA is the binding sale and purchase contract. The MYBA Memorandum of Agreement is the most common form across the Mediterranean and Caribbean markets; the IYBA form is used in the Americas. Key clauses to settle with independent counsel: title warranties, inventory matching the sale, deficiencies remediated or priced, an acceptance protocol with adequate time, governing law clause not the seller’s home jurisdiction, and a closing schedule resistant to acceleration. Hill Dickinson, Watson Farley & Williams, Ince, Stephenson Harwood and Reed Smith are recognised firms.

04-acquisition-process.question: What flag should I register a private yacht under?
04-acquisition-process.answer: Selection depends on four things in combination: compliance, charter intent, financing, and owner residence. Cayman Islands is a Red Ensign Group Category 1 register with MCA-equivalent oversight. Marshall Islands offers an open registry with 84 days commercial use under Yacht Engaged in Trade or Private Yacht Limited Charter regimes. Malta is the EU flag of choice for owners who want EU charter operation, often alongside its leasing arrangement for VAT. Red Ensign Group includes Isle of Man, Bermuda, Gibraltar, BVI, and Cayman in Category 1; Jersey and Guernsey are Category 2 registers, limited to vessels of up to 150 GT, or up to 400 GT where UK-standard survey arrangements are in place.

05-new-build-versus-brokerage.question: Should I buy a new yacht or a brokerage yacht?
05-new-build-versus-brokerage.answer: The threshold tests are: a hold horizon of seven to ten years on paper, a use that no brokerage yacht meets, and commitment to four things (independent owner’s representative engaged before contract, specialist shipbuilding counsel, technical due diligence on the yard’s order book and financial condition, willingness to push back on the yard’s first-draft contract). If a brokerage yacht meets most of the intended use, building is justified only if the rest matters to the buyer. Below seven years’ hold, the new build cost premium does not amortise.

05-new-build-versus-brokerage.question: What does an owner’s representative do on a yacht new build?
05-new-build-versus-brokerage.answer: The owner’s representative manages the buyer’s interests across yard selection, contract drafting, technical specification, build supervision, milestone inspection, snag-listing, and delivery acceptance. The representative should be paid by the buyer, and any yard commission, broker referral or fee contingent on closing should be disclosed to the buyer in writing, with its amount and payer, before engagement. SYBAss, with IAMI and GUEST, set up the Yacht Owner Representative Programme (announced June 2023) and the Yacht Owner’s Representative Register (launched November 2024), which the Superyacht Alliance for Professional Standards administers to vet practitioners.

05-new-build-versus-brokerage.question: What stage payment schedule is typical on a yacht new build?
05-new-build-versus-brokerage.answer: Commercial shipbuilding puts 40 percent or more of the price before delivery (Watson Farley & Williams); custom yacht schedules routinely require well over half before delivery, and up to 90 percent on some projects. The balance is paid at delivery and final acceptance. Refund guarantee credit quality is the buyer’s main protection: a tier-one bank pay-on-demand guarantee is the standard to ask for; surety wrappers are weaker. Liquidated damages are typically 1 percent of contract value per week of delay, capped at 5 to 10 percent. Force majeure burden on the yard to prove but-for causation per English law is the practitioner standard.

05-new-build-versus-brokerage.question: Why does the quality of owner’s representation matter?
05-new-build-versus-brokerage.answer: SYBAss announced the Yacht Owner Representative Programme with IAMI and GUEST in June 2023 because the yards reported that some owner’s representatives had no clear idea of what the role required; the Yacht Owner’s Representative Register followed in November 2024. Jack Inglis of ULTIMAR has published a case in which a family office CFO acted as deputised owner’s representative; the delivery snag list exceeded 1,200 items against the family office’s reported figure of around 100. Brokers, yards and management companies also have established relationships with each other, so the buyer benefits from one adviser who is paid by the buyer and discloses any other payment in writing.

05-new-build-versus-brokerage.question: How do I check if an owner’s representative is on the YOR Register?
05-new-build-versus-brokerage.answer: The Yacht Owner’s Representative Register (YORR) is the cross-industry list of vetted owner’s representatives. The register table is published by the Superyacht Alliance for Professional Standards at https://superyachtalliance.org/register/register-table/ and is searchable by firm and by named principal. Applicants either complete all four YORP courses, more than 200 hours in total, or show at least three completed new build projects over 30 metres as owner’s representative and complete Unit 40. Experienced representatives can register by that second route only until 30 June 2027. Every applicant endorses a code of conduct, which requires any commission to be disclosed in writing, and a committee checks CVs, references and conflicts of interest. Buyers considering an owner’s representative can look up the firm and its principals on the register table directly before signing any engagement letter.

06-refit.question: How much does a superyacht refit cost?
06-refit.answer: A five-year survey or major refit typically runs 5 to 15 percent of insured hull value, depending on scope. On the publisher’s project archive a mid-life refit runs EUR 10,000 to 30,000 per metre and a major structural refit EUR 40,000 to 100,000 or more per metre, so EUR 2 to 5 million on a 50 metre yacht. Annual maintenance runs EUR 2,000 to 8,000 per metre a year. Overruns of 30 to 50 percent against the original quote are common. Part is work that could not be seen when the yacht was quoted, which a contingency of 10 to 25 percent covers; the rest comes from loose specification and weak project management, which the contract and the owner’s representative should contain. Above 30 percent of pre-refit market value, a practitioner rule of thumb suggests considering a sale.

06-refit.question: When should I refit a yacht versus selling it?
06-refit.answer: A practitioner rule of thumb, not a market rule: if the projected refit cost exceeds 30 percent of the yacht’s pre-refit market value, selling is worth considering. Below that, refit is the usual path. The calculation differs for every yacht. Set out on paper how well the refitted yacht will suit the owner’s continuing use, alongside the cost of selling and buying a comparable yacht: depreciation, transaction costs, and the loss of an established crew. The threshold is rough; the decision is the owner’s, taken with the independent adviser.

06-refit.question: Which are the best refit yards for superyachts?
06-refit.answer: Northern European refit specialists include Pendennis (Falmouth), Damen Vlissingen, Royal Huisman (Vollenhove) and Lürssen (Hamburg). Mediterranean refit yards include MB92 Group (Barcelona and La Ciotat), STP and Astilleros de Mallorca (Palma), Lusben (Viareggio), Amico & Co (Genoa) and the Palumbo Superyachts network. Top European yards are typically booked 12 to 24 months ahead for major refits, so book as far ahead as the chosen yard’s order book runs. Select on track record with similar yachts and the project manager’s experience, not on the cheapest quote.

06-refit.question: What is Spanish Inward Processing Relief for yachts?
06-refit.answer: Spanish IPR (Inward Processing Relief, the régimen de perfeccionamiento activo) is the customs procedure under which a non-EU-flagged yacht can be refitted in Spain with the 21 percent VAT on the works exempt, provided the procedure is followed through to the yacht’s departure from the EU. It is separate from temporary admission, which covers the yacht’s use in EU waters and ordinary repair and maintenance but not a structural refit. Authorisation must be in place before the works begin, through the yard or an agent with the correct customs status, and compliance rests with the owner rather than the yard. If the procedure is not followed, VAT can fall due on the works and potentially on the yacht itself, with interest and penalties. MB92, Astilleros de Mallorca and several smaller Spanish yards are equipped for it. France and Italy treat refit VAT under different rules. Independent counsel should select the VAT structure for the specific refit scope.

06-refit.question: How do I sell a superyacht?
06-refit.answer: Most sellers appoint a central agent: one broker, under a fixed-term exclusive agreement, who markets the yacht while other brokers introduce buyers. The seller’s own lawyer should review that agreement, in particular the minimum marketing activity, the commission payable after it ends, and the governing law (Clyde & Co, The Guide to Superyacht Law). Before listing, assemble the maintenance records, the class status and the evidence of the yacht’s VAT position, and set the asking price against published days on market for the size band. The sale is usually made on the MYBA Memorandum of Agreement, with a deposit of typically 10 percent on signing.

06-refit.question: What does selling a yacht cost?
06-refit.answer: The main cost is the broker’s commission, paid by the seller from the proceeds. Two norms are in use: the US flat 10 percent of the sale price, and the MYBA sliding scale of 10 percent on the first 10 million, 5 percent on the second 10 million and 2.5 percent above. On a EUR 28 million sale that is EUR 2.8 million, or about EUR 1.7 million. A buyer’s broker is paid out of the seller’s commission, typically half of it or a little less. Agree the scale, any split, and any commission payable after the agreement ends in writing before listing. The seller’s own legal fees come on top.

06-refit.question: What warranties does a seller give when selling a yacht?
06-refit.answer: Under the MYBA Memorandum of Agreement the seller’s warranties are narrow: the right to sell, and delivery free of mortgages, liens and other claims, with exclusion clauses ruling out warranties on condition beyond what the agreement states (Andrew Charlier of HFW, in BOAT International, September 2025). The 2021 MYBA E-MoA also has the seller warrant that no undischarged tax or VAT liability has been incurred. The warranties are usually backed by a guarantee from the beneficial owner or a company on its behalf. Its scope, cap and expiry are negotiated, so the seller’s lawyer should agree them before signing.

07-operations.question: What does a superyacht captain earn in 2026?
07-operations.answer: Per the YPI Crew 2026 salary guide, a captain on a 50 metre yacht earns EUR 10,000 to 16,000 per month. A captain on an 80 metre yacht earns EUR 16,000 to 23,000. Quay Crew’s 2025/26 captain survey records a 7 percent increase in the 70 to 79 metre bracket since its 2023 survey, and 63 percent of captains surveyed on time-for-time rotation. Experienced senior crew, captains above all, are in shortest supply; their pay continues to rise where junior crew pay has plateaued. Crew accounts for 30 to 40 percent of total annual operating cost.

07-operations.question: How many crew does a 50m superyacht need?
07-operations.answer: On practitioner figures, a 50 metre motor yacht in private use typically carries 12 to 16 crew and a 50 metre sailing yacht 9 to 12. Published guides give leaner minimums: YachtBuyer suggests 8 to 12 across the 40 to 50 metre band. Manning levels are set by the flag state’s Minimum Safe Manning Certificate, with senior officers requiring Certificates of Competency and STCW endorsements. On commercially operated yachts, MLC 2006 governs working hours, accommodation, and contracts; amendments expected in force on 23 December 2027 add requirements on shore leave, repatriation and harassment. The captain hire also affects the other operating decisions; a candidate who questions the owner’s plans on itinerary, maintenance, budget and crew in interview is often the stronger hire.

07-operations.question: What insurance does a superyacht need?
07-operations.answer: Hull insurance at 0.7 to 1.5 percent of insured value for a well-maintained 40 to 50 metre yacht. P&I cover for crew injury, environmental liability, third-party, and charter guest claims at USD 500 million third-party limit through Shipowners’ Club or Steamship Mutual. Competitive quotes from at least three brokers with over-30 metre yacht experience before binding, each with its commission disclosed in writing. Builder’s risk insurance during refit, with the owner co-insured under a waiver of subrogation rather than only noted, a sum insured covering the whole vessel, and cover in transit between subcontractor sites; the owner’s own hull policy usually suspends or limits cover while the yacht is in the yard.

07-operations.question: Should I operate my yacht as a charter yacht?
07-operations.answer: For most charter operations, charter income covers part of the cost of ownership, not all of it. The first-time owner benefits from three years of private operation before introducing charter. Practitioners usually wait until year four before converting a privately operated yacht to charter, by which time the owner has three years of actual use to go on. If charter is being considered from year one, work a case based on yacht size, weekly rate, and weeks against the BOAT International published cases set out in chapter 1. The yields in the published case studies depend on releasing prime-season weeks (mid-July to mid-August in the Mediterranean), so the owner needs to decide early whether to release them.

08-motor-versus-sail.question: Is it cheaper to own a sailing yacht than a motor yacht?
08-motor-versus-sail.answer: On a 50 metre yacht, a motor yacht at 400 cruising hours a year burns EUR 200,000 to 350,000 of fuel; a sailing yacht of the same length operated mainly under sail burns EUR 60,000 to 120,000. Crew complement is 9 to 12 on the sailing yacht against 12 to 16 on the motor. On the chapter’s 35 metre figures, a quality sailing yacht comes in about a fifth to a third below the equivalent motor programme on total seven-year cost (capex plus opex minus residual), and 25 to 40 percent below where it holds its value better. Net annual maintenance is broadly comparable, although more of the sailing yacht’s comes as large sums at long intervals, for sails and rigging.

08-motor-versus-sail.question: What is a hybrid superyacht?
08-motor-versus-sail.answer: Hybrid drive combines diesel power with electric motors and a battery hotel-load capability, allowing the yacht to operate at low load on battery power and dock without the generator running. Heesen’s FDHF (Fast Displacement Hybrid Format), Sanlorenzo’s SX line, and equivalent programmes from Lürssen and Royal Huisman are the production references. Royal Huisman’s 65 metre Aquarius II, delivered in 2025, is the sailing reference for semi-hybrid generation with battery load smoothing. A hybrid costs less to run and emits less carbon than a conventional motor yacht, but more than a sailing yacht.

08-motor-versus-sail.question: Does the EU ETS apply to private superyachts?
08-motor-versus-sail.answer: Only in limited cases. EU ETS Maritime applies to ships of 5,000 GT and above carrying passengers or cargo for commercial purposes. A privately used yacht is outside the system at any size, and most yachts, including 60 to 80 metre motor yachts, are far below 5,000 GT in any case. A very large yacht on commercial charter can fall inside it. The share of emissions paid for rose from 40 percent (2024) and 70 percent (2025) to 100 percent from 2026 emissions onward. A Commission proposal of July 2026 would bring some ship types of 400 to 5,000 GT into the system from 2031; yachts are not among those named. HVO (hydrotreated vegetable oil) is a drop-in diesel replacement with a lifecycle greenhouse gas reduction of up to about 90 percent where certified waste-derived supply is available; exhaust CO2 is much the same as diesel’s.

09-decision-framework.question: What questions should I ask before buying a yacht?
09-decision-framework.answer: The ten questions in chapter nine of The First Owner’s Reference set out what to ask. Who introduced the yacht and who pays them. Who recommended the lawyer, the surveyor, the management company, and who pays them. Has any party offered services at no cost, and who is paying them. Has every party disclosed their commercial relationships in writing including referral fees, retrocessions, and equity holdings. Is legal counsel independent of the broker, the yard, and the management company. Is the surveyor independent of the seller and broker. Is the owner’s representative paid by the owner, with any contingent fee, yard commission or referral relationship disclosed in writing.

09-decision-framework.question: How do I find an independent yacht owner’s representative?
09-decision-framework.answer: The test is independence from yards, brokers, and management companies: income paid by the owner, and any commission or payment contingent on a closed transaction disclosed to the owner in writing in advance. Firms working as owner’s representatives paid only by the owner include A2B Marine Projects, ULTIMAR, Divergent Yachting, Mariner Technical Services, JMS Yachting, ABL Yachts, KRM Yacht, Saor Alba, Occam Naval Architecture and Project Management, and Foreland Marine, the publisher of this reference. The Yacht Owner’s Representative Register, launched in November 2024 and administered by the Superyacht Alliance for Professional Standards, is the cross-industry vetting register.

09-decision-framework.question: How do I know if a yacht adviser is conflicted?
09-decision-framework.answer: A useful test is whether a party would walk away from a deal that did not benefit the buyer. An adviser paid only by the buyer, with nothing that depends on the deal closing, has no financial reason not to. Brokerages with new build arms (Edmiston, Burgess, Y.CO, Ocean Independence, Camper & Nicholsons, Fraser, Cecil Wright, Moran), yacht management firms extending into new build, and naval architects acting as owner’s representatives can carry conflicts: the same group may have introduced the yard and may be paid by it. The book’s standard is written disclosure of any such payment, its amount and who makes it; the buyer then weighs the advice against it.

09-decision-framework.question: Do you pay VAT when buying a superyacht as a non-EU resident?
09-decision-framework.answer: A non-EU resident using the yacht privately can often avoid paying VAT on the purchase by operating under Temporary Admission relief, which lets a non-EU-owned yacht cruise in EU waters without importing it, provided the eligibility and time-limit conditions are met. If the yacht is imported, or the owner is EU-resident, VAT is generally due unless another relief applies. As chapter nine sets out, the ownership structure, VAT position, and importation strategy have to be decided together from the outset; getting the sequence wrong exposes the owner to liabilities and penalties calculated on the value of the yacht.

09-decision-framework.question: Isle of Man or Malta for yacht ownership?
09-decision-framework.answer: Neither is universally better; the right jurisdiction depends on the owner’s use, residency and tax position, financing, and succession plans. The Isle of Man is a long-established superyacht jurisdiction with a mature professional services sector, though Quadrant Group estimates an Isle of Man structure is the right answer for only around a quarter of purchases. Malta is often more appropriate for an EU-resident owner who wants VAT-paid certainty within Europe. The British Virgin Islands and the Cayman Islands are further established alternatives. Jurisdiction should be the outcome of the planning, not the starting point.

09-decision-framework.question: What does a corporate services provider do for a yacht owner?
09-decision-framework.answer: A corporate services provider designs and administers the ownership structure: maintaining the ownership vehicle, meeting statutory and regulatory obligations, and coordinating the banks, flag administrations, insurers, lawyers, and tax advisers around the yacht. It typically becomes the central point through which those relationships are managed across the life of the asset, and it helps separate the owner’s personal assets from the yacht, providing legal protection should liabilities arise. Fees are charged either on a fixed annual basis or by time spent; owners should understand which model applies.

09-decision-framework.question: Should a yacht be registered privately or commercially?
09-decision-framework.answer: It depends on how the owner intends to use the yacht. Commercial registration is not simply a way to offset running costs with charter income; chartering is closer to operating a business, with additional regulatory, tax, and operational obligations, and the owner pays VAT on their own time aboard. Private ownership deserves the same scrutiny before it is assumed to be simpler. The decision should follow genuine intended use rather than what the yacht could do, with flexibility built in where plans may change.

09-decision-framework.question: What is Temporary Admission relief for yachts?
09-decision-framework.answer: Temporary Admission is a customs relief that allows a yacht owned by a non-EU resident to be used in EU waters for a limited period without paying import VAT, provided the conditions are met, including that the yacht is not placed at the disposal of an EU resident and is re-exported within the permitted time. It is commonly used for private, non-EU-owned yachts cruising the Mediterranean, and is one of the broad ownership models set out in chapter nine.
